claim: At a 32K training sequence length, sparse attention of the DSA/LSA lineage is a net loss versus dense MLA: 1.08x forward, 0.79x backward, 0.83x total per attention layer, with the crossover to a win only at 64K.
stance_target: The repo's verdict that CSA2 at 32k is 'the axis most likely to disappoint'
scope_conditions: Per-layer training latency microbenchmark, fixed sequence lengths, on the authors' AI accelerators; context-parallel degrees 4/8/16/32/128 at 32K/64K/128K/256K/1024K
quoted_support: At short sequence lengths (< 64K), dense MLA runs faster because LSA incurs indexing overheads (yielding a net latency of 0.83x at 32K). However, beyond 64K, the quadratic scaling of dense MLA takes over - especially in the backward pass - allowing LSA to reverse the gap sharply, reaching up to a 7.73x speedup at 1024K.

claim: With variable-length sequence packing in a real data mixture, the practical training-efficiency crossover between sparse and dense attention moves from 64K to 128K — so at 32k the sparse path is further behind than the fixed-length microbenchmark suggests.
stance_target: The repo's claim that CSA2's 1M-context published wins do not transfer to 32k training
scope_conditions: Authors' actual data mixture with variable-length packing
quoted_support: Note that these microbenchmarks are measured with fixed sequence lengths; when accounting for variable-length sequence packing in our actual data mixture, the practical efficiency crossover occurs at 128K.

claim: The sparse-attention operator is severely memory-bound, achieving only about 4.5% of peak HBM bandwidth (~1/22) because each selected token is fetched by an independent gather of a 1,152 B BF16 latent KV vector spanning only 3 cachelines, giving ~6% memory-level parallelism and ~75% cacheline packing efficiency.
stance_target: The claim that sparse attention's theoretical FLOP savings do not translate into proportional wall-clock savings
scope_conditions: Operator-level profiling of the SFA sparse-attention kernel; BF16 latent KV of 1,152 B per token
quoted_support: each selected token is fetched via an independent gather of a single latent KV vector (1,152 B in BF16), which spans only 3 cachelines. Consequently, two inefficiencies compound: first, this gather occupies merely 3 of the ~50 outstanding memory slots (yielding ~6% memory-level parallelism); second, even within these 3 cachelines, data packing efficiency is only ~75%. The resulting net effective bandwidth thus plummets to a mere ~4.5% (~1/22) of peak performance.
numbers: 1,152 B per BF16 latent KV vector

claim: The sparse-attention backward pass is worse than the forward pass: gradient accumulation allocates a full-sequence-length HBM buffer and executes scatter_add over the selected sparse index set, and cores selecting overlapping indices serialize writes to shared cachelines; the indexer backward suffers the same cross-core serialization across all L scored positions.
stance_target: The claim that sparse attention's training cost is dominated by the backward pass, not the forward pass
scope_conditions: SFA backward pass profiling; applies to training, not inference
quoted_support: this output discontiguity inflicts a more severe performance penalty during training. In the backward pass, gradient updates rely on scatter_add operations over the identical non-contiguous token indices. Due to the scattered nature and input-dependent selection of these indices, independent computing cores frequently attempt to write to overlapping KV gradient regions in HBM.

stance_target: Any training-step cost model that treats attention forward and backward as comparable

claim: The indexer accounts for up to 90% of per-layer latency at a 1024K context length, and its latency grows 27x (0.034 ms to 0.930 ms) while sparse-attention latency stays nearly constant at ~0.10 ms.
stance_target: The claim that at long context the indexer, not the sparse attention operator, is the bottleneck
scope_conditions: Per-layer latency breakdown vs context length; Lightning Indexer (LI) vs SFA
quoted_support: as the context grows, accounting for up to 90% of the per-layer latency at a 1024K context length. ... SFA latency remains nearly constant at ~0.10 ms, whereas LI latency increases by 27x, from 0.034 ms to 0.930 ms.
numbers: up to 90% of per-layer latency at 1024K

claim: Adjacent transformer layers share 57.4% of their Top-K budget on average, and reusing an adjacent layer's index set still captures 93.2% of the target layer's attention mass — the empirical basis for cross-layer index reuse.
stance_target: CSA2's Reuse mode and IndexCache-style cross-layer index sharing

quoted_support: Adjacent layers share 57.4% of their Top-K budget on average. Despite this partial overlap, reusing an adjacent layer's index set still captures 93.2% of the target layer's attention mass.

claim: The standard DSA-lineage training recipe is two-stage: a dense warm-up where the indexer is supervised against the full-sequence attention distribution, then sparse training where the distillation target is the attention distribution renormalized over the selected subset, with sink and SWA tokens deliberately included in the target because they carry substantial attention mass.
stance_target: The repo's claim that top-k selection is non-differentiable and the indexer needs a separate distillation loss
scope_conditions: Section 2.2 two-stage training; Eq. (4) distillation loss
quoted_support: the dense warm-up stage requires no modification: the indexer is supervised against the full-sequence attention distribution (Eq. (4)). In the sparse training stage, the distillation target becomes the attention distribution renormalized over the selected subset St. ... during training we deliberately distill the indexer over the entire selected set, including the sink and SWA portions.

claim: The fixed-to-sparse attention budget is split roughly 1:1 (Ksink=16, Kswa=1024, Ksparse=1024), so about 50% of selected tokens sit in contiguous memory regions — a deliberate hardware-alignment choice, not a quality-driven one.
stance_target: How a sparse-attention budget should be split for hardware efficiency
quoted_support: We set sink size Ksink = 16 and sliding window size Kswa = 1024, yielding a fixed-to-sparse budget ratio of approximately 1:1 (determined by ablation, see Section 5.3), which makes roughly 50% of the selected tokens reside in contiguous memory regions.

claim: LSA supports native training with context lengths up to one million tokens and underpins LongCat-2.0 (1.6T-A48B), with scaling experiments spanning 69B-A3B to 560B-A27B models and an open-sourced LongCat-Flash-Lite-Sparse (69B-A3B).
stance_target: That sparse attention is trainable at production scale, not only at inference
scope_conditions: Production training runs at Meituan LongCat; 69B-A3B to 560B-A27B
quoted_support: Extensive scaling experiments, ranging from 69B-A3B to 560B-A27B models, demonstrate that LSA consistently achieves performance on par with full attention across both general-purpose and long-context benchmarks. Moreover, LSA supports native training with context lengths of up to one million tokens and underpins the development of LongCat-2.0 (1.6T-A48B).

claim: Full-layer speedups are much smaller than core-attention speedups once indexer overhead is included: core attention gains 1.56-1.69x in prefill and 1.11-1.26x in decode, but the full layer peaks at 1.49x prefill (4K) and 1.14x decode (8K) and decays to 1.02-1.04x at longer contexts.
stance_target: The claim that indexer overhead eats most of the sparse-attention kernel win
scope_conditions: Table 3 inference settings, BF16, K=2048, prefill qlen=2048, decode batch=4/qlen=1
quoted_support: At the core-attention level, HFA achieves consistent speedups of 1.56-1.69x during prefill and 1.11-1.26x during decode. After including indexer overhead, however, the full-layer speedup becomes increasingly constrained by indexing cost, reaching a peak of 1.49x for prefill at 4K context and 1.14x for decode at 8K context, before gradually diminishing to 1.02-1.04x at longer contexts.
